#3438. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3437. Texas Goes Blue: James Talarico Triumphs Over Ken Paxton

The myth of a blue Texas is now a reality.

Democrat James Talarico has defeated Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the year. Shortly after Talarico was projected to win, Democrat Gina Hinojosa was projected the winner over longtime Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

The victories marks a seismic shift in Texas politics, and in the nation’s current political map, ending a 32-year statewide drought for Democrats in the Republican stronghold. The party now controls the state’s governership, as well as a U.S. Senate seat there for at least the next six years.

The Senate race started with two bitter primaries, with Talarico defeating Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) on the Democratic side, and Paxton defeating incumbent Senator John Cornyn after landing Donald Trump’s endorsement. Cornyn refused to endorse his party’s nominee after losing the primary, citing Paxton’s long record of corruption and abuse of office. In audio leaked to Rolling Stone last month, Paxton griped about how much the contentious primary with Paxton hurt his chances.

Cornyn was one of the first to celebrate Talarico’s win on Tuesday. “The voters have spoken, and I want to extend my congratulations to James Talarico on his election to the U.S. Senate,” he wrote. “I look forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Throughout most of the general election campaign, Talarico held a polling lead over Paxton. The upstart candidate barnstormed the state for months before Paxton even began to put on his campaigning shoes. Talarico, a state House member, ran on an economically progressive platform focused on cost of living issues and anti-corruption. Paxton, a poster boy for corruption, ran largely on his allegiance to Trump while trying to paint Talarico as a radical leftist.

Talarico sought to take advantage of a uniquely abysmal landscape for Republicans across the country to steal a seat for Democrats in a state that voted for Trump by a 13-point margin in 2024. Trump, ironically enough, turned out to be Talarico’s biggest campaign asset. The president’s approval numbers tanked when he launched his war against Iran this spring — breaking his “no more wars” campaign promise and sending the price of fuel skyrocketing. It hasn’t exactly been a winning strategy. Inflation is up, wage growth is stagnant, and Americans can’t afford the life their parents had. At the same time, Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire dumped almost half a billion dollars into Republican reelection efforts — much of it into Texas.Paxton, like many Texas Republicans, spent the campaign operating under the assumption that just being the GOP nominee would be enough to notch a win. Paxton ducked the three proposed network debates between himself and Talarico, studiously avoided interactions with any press not explicitly aligned with the right, and struggled to develop any level of compelling personal charm over the course of the race.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Trump’s support of Paxton — over an incumbent Republican and the objections of Senate GOP leaders —  elevated the Texas race into a referendum on Trumpism writ large. The president campaigned throughout the state alongside Paxton, including hosting an “emergency” midterm republican convention in Dallas, Texas. Paxton was then caught complaining in leaked audio that the president’s appearance had hurt his numbers. Unable to distance himself from the president, Paxton and his allies attempted to reframe the race towards culture war fear mongering. Here’s How the Key Races Are Breaking How to Livestream Midterm Election-Night News for Free Without Cable

Despite the monetary advantages held by the GOP, Trump has shed basically all the support he managed to accumulate among disaffected Hispanic voters during the 2024 election — a critical constituency within Texas. Early voting data indicated that enthusiasm among Republican voters was trailing Democrats.

The candidates spent the final hours of the campaign making last-second pitches to voters, offering vastly competing visions for the state and nation.

At a Monday concert rally in the heart of Austin, Talarico and Hinojosa spoke before a full house crowd of almost 2,000 people. Talarico, swimming against a three-decade long tide of GOP rule in the state, reminded his supporters of the Texas of yore — and the Democrats who shaped it.

“We are the state that pioneered ranching and energy and computers. We are the state that gave this country Barbara Jordan, Anne Richards, LBJ and the great society,” Talarico said. “We are the state that put breakfast in a taco. There is nothing we can’t do.”

The Democrat contrasted his vision of the state with the governance of state and federal Republican leadership. “We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” Talarico said, repeatedly referencing Ken Paxton’s extensive record of profiteering and abuse of office. “This election should be about chasing a vision of what this state can be. Texas public schools that are the envy of the nation. A Texas economy that is second to none and Texas families that are stronger and healthier than they have ever been before. This won’t happen overnight, but a giant state deserves giant dreams.”

Paxton was originally scheduled to close his “Come and Take It” campaign tour with a large rally at The Alamo — a historic landmark of the Texas Revolution famously taken by the Mexican force. Paxton cancelled the rally and instead shifted his event to Allen, Texas, in the suburbs of Dallas.

The state attorney general’s closing pitch to voters was decidedly less rosy. In front of a much smaller crowd, Paxton warned of the threats of socialism, transgender inclusive healthcare, men in women’s sports, unfettered mass immigration, and a whole host of culture war priorities that had so far failed to secure him a major lead in the polls.  Trending Stories Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and 'You Can See Everything' Mick Jagger Praises Sam Fender’s Rolling Stones Cover Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

“We are all sinners and we all need you,” Paxton told supporters in a prayer ahead of his speech.

In the end, not enough Texans bought Paxton’s pitch.

#3433. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3431. Abdul El-Sayed Handily Beats Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate Race

Abdul El-Sayed has made history, becoming the country's first-ever Muslim senator ... after he handily defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan.

NBC News reported overnight that El-Sayed was the projected winner in the hard-fought race for the Michigan Senate seat, clocking in with 52.3 percent of the vote, compared to Rogers' 45.7 percent with 94.4 percent of votes counted.

In total, El-Sayed has so far raked in 2,431,112 votes to Rogers' 2,123,522 votes, with the third candidate, Lydia Christensen, only getting 1 percent of the vote.

#3429. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3428. AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into the App Store

Hundreds of AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into Apple’s App Store after passing app review. The same apps were also available in the Google Play Store.

An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims …

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

I feel like this going to be a never ending cat and mouse game. Much like Apple has always had with jailbreaks.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

#3425. Kansas Elects Its First Democratic Senator in 94 Years

Methodist minister Adam Hamiliton, a Democrat, has defeated Republican Roger Marshall in the race to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate, ending a Democratic dry spell that has lasted nearly a century.

The mild-mannered megachurch pastor, who has been registered as a Republican, a Democrat, and an Independent over the course of his lifetime, assembled a broad coalition of voters in the heartland state, en route to pulling off one of the most improbable wins of the year in a state Donald Trump carried by over 16 percent just two years ago.

Marshall sought to paint his rival, the founding pastor of the largest united Methodist church in the country,  as “too woke” and “too weak” to represent Kansas, but voters appeared receptive to Hamiliton’s brand of scripture-laced centrism. “I’m pretty sure if Jesus were here [Marshall would] consider him too woke,” Hamilton said during his campaign.

In 2020, Marshall was re-elected with a margin of more than 11 points. This year, a surprisingly strong challenge from Hamilton, a difficult environment for Republicans, and new reporting about Marshall’s aggressive efforts to recoup payment from patients he treated when he was a practicing OB-GYN proved too much for the GOP nominee to overcome.

In polls throughout the election cycle, voters in Kansas consistently and overwhelmingly pointed to the economy as their top concern. In a state where nearly 90 percent of land is used for farming and ranching, the Republican candidate was damaged by the rising price of diesel gas — a side effect of the U.S. ongoing war with Iran — as well as the president’s decision to allow beef to be imported into the country at lower tariff rates.

Marshall, who was an OB-GYN before running for Senate, was hurt by the revelations that he had filed lawsuits against hundreds of patients who failed to pay their medical bills. The New York Times reported in September that at least 81 of Marshall’s patients were arrested for missing court dates related to their debts, including a pregnant woman with a 2-year-old daughter. That woman, Meischa Zimmerman, had been uninsured when Marshall delivered her child via a c-section in 2009; she was arrested three times as Marshall pursued payment. #3424. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

Today we’re delivering it: a fully-fledged, professional app built for touch.”

Being able to carry out all of the work within a single app on a single file is a key attraction of Affinity. The integrated app replaces the separate Affinity Photo, Affinity Publisher, and Affinity Designer apps.

Sketch: Rough out concepts the moment they land, with the unique capabilities of Apple Pencil like pressure and tilt in every mark, thick where you press and soft where you tilt. A full brush library comes with controls to shape each brush into the exact tool you need. Sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again.

Vector: Responsive, smooth and under control. Build a full logo or icon system with real curves and precise nodes, or bring a rough drawing through from Sketch. Sketch to Shapes turns hand-drawn forms into clean vector shapes.

Photo: Fine-tune RAW files, make intelligent selections, retouch in real time and build full composites at the shoot or on the go. Users can even sketch over a photo first to plan where a subject or prop should sit. The Mask Tool finds the boundary as the Apple Pencil pixel precision runs along a challenging edge, so hair, fur and foliage take a stroke rather than an afternoon. Every mask, grade and retouch stays live and undoable, even thousands of layers deep.

Layout: Create multi-page documents such as ‘zines, lookbooks and photo books, with text and images flowing across pages; master pages and grids keep everything consistent, and typography exactly right. Projects go all the way to a print-ready file with proper colour handling.

Canva says the app supports all of the advanced capabilities of Apple Pencil Pro: pressure, tilt, barrel roll, squeeze, and hover. AI features include generative expand, upscaling resolution, and adding attributes like motion blur. A Decompose Layer feature even splits a flat image into editable layers.

Affinity for iPad is a free download from the App Store.

While none of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s three modes are perfect, they’re all solid enough to deliver a well-rounded experience anchored by the franchise's incredible gunplay.

DMZ mode is solid and has potential to get better

DMZ mode is a little more PVP than I’d like

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Platforms: Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S (reviewed)Price: $69 / £69 / AU$109Release Date: October 23, 2026Genre: First-person shooter

The Call of Duty season has arrived, and this year Infinity Ward is back in the driver’s seat. After back-to-back Black Ops games, Activision’s FPS cash cow returns to the Modern Warfare moniker and gameplay style, which I've always preferred (not that I dislike Black Ops; I just prefer MW's cast of characters and gameplay).

Modern Warfare 4 feels like a return to form for the long-running franchise, both in the single-player campaign and in the overall gunplay. The time-to-kill is a little longer than in the last couple of games, letting you use more inventive tactics in firefights. It’s not just about who shot who first. And I’m genuinely torn. It doesn’t feel like what I’m used to from the franchise, but maybe that’s not such a bad thing.

If you never liked COD games, nothing here will change your mind, but if you’re a lapsed fan of the series who wants to see how Captain Price’s story ties up and still enjoy a fun first-person shooter, this might be the one to come back to.

I'm generally not a Call of Duty campaign fan. I usually play a few hours a year and spend the rest of the time longing for multiplayer, so I fizzle out about halfway through. Which is why I was shocked when the Modern Warfare 4 campaign actually hooked me right off the bat and kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through.

Sure, the story is a little convoluted, especially the Price portion, which has the unenviable task of cleaning up the mess left by the last few Call of Duty: Modern Warfare games. But I think it does a fantastic job of tying up all the loose ends into a coherent story that successfully caps Price’s story (at least until the next time Modern Warfare gets rebooted).

Price’s missions take place five days before the story’s other half (you’re essentially playing two campaigns at once and switching back and forth). His story crescendos with the start of the other plot and a massive Korean invasion.

Price’s story will make you feel like Jason Statham or John Wick, running around shooting and fighting in first-person hand-to-hand combat. The Korean story has a more traditional war-game feel and follows Park Hyun Jun and his squad. They’re entertaining, with a mix of Korean and US soldiers who add lighthearted humor during intense frontline moments.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The two interwoven stories contrast in a way that makes this the best Call of Duty campaign since 2009’s Modern Warfare 2.

Both sides of the campaign can get a little dark and heavy. An early scene puts you in the shoes of an invader on the Korean side, forcing difficult decisions that can make you wonder if you're the hero or villain (or somewhere in the gray middle ground). For example, an early Price fight scene ends in pure and utter brutality.

Then there’s the heavily hyped Stranded mission, a ramped-up version of the DMZ mode with a story and characters you actually care about. While most of the campaign is linear, this mission gives you a level of freedom we don’t often see in COD games. It’s dripping with tension and best of all, it’s fun. It was a dangerous call for Infinity Ward to include one mission that stands out, as it risked making the rest of the campaign feel inferior. However, because the more traditional COD missions are also so well executed and the stakes feel so high, this problem is negated.

I got seriously into Arc Raiders for about a month before some updates made me fall off. It was my first taste of an extraction shooter, and it felt good to return to the genre with DMZ mode. It’s definitely the weakest of the three main modes in Modern Warfare 4, but it’s still fun.

We already know the extraction formula is successful. In my opinion, Call of Duty is the best first-person shooter franchise from a pure gunplay perspective, so it makes sense that smooshing the two together would lead to a solid online mode.

The missions in DMZ are relatively generic and basic, but they’re motivation enough to keep you moving through a session beyond just grabbing the best loot and extracting.

My only issue with DMZ comes from the overall COD culture. Years of competitive multiplayer have created a shoot-first mentality that removes much of the tension that comes from talking to people in other extraction shooters. I love the “hey, are you cool?” interactions I experienced in Arc Raiders (and even in the Dark Zone of The Division), and in the DMZ matches I played for this review, every encounter with other players was instantly hostile.

The thrill of finding loot and getting out at an extraction point is as satisfying as any other game in the genre (perhaps even more so, because getting your loot almost certainly involved fighting another player who attacked as you tried to extract).

And while there wasn’t much in the way of enemy negotiations, I had great experiences with other players in my squad. In almost every match, my random squadmates cared as much about my survival and successful extraction as I did.

I look forward to seeing how Infinity Ward builds on DMZ, both in this Modern Warfare 4 and across future COD titles.

For me, this is the main event of any Call of Duty game. Sure, the campaign is fun for eight hours or so, and other modes like Black Ops’ Zombies and DMZ will hook a certain percentage of the player base; it’s multiplayer that has made this franchise one of the biggest in gaming history.

And while it had a few small flaws at launch (erratic spawns and skill-based matchmaking being all over the place with so many new players), the overall experience is there, and it’s great. The guns are fun to level up and add new attachments (the usual slots are all there), and it even adds new modes that borrow from other FPS games, like Collateral, a round-based plant-and-defuse mode with buy stages like Counter-Strike. It’s a well-executed game mode that feels fresh even if it’s been done before outside of COD.

Frontline is a spawn-campers' dream. Instead of spawning in logical, somewhat “safe” locations, you only spawn in your base. This becomes a problem when you’re on the losing team, because the other squad knows exactly where you’ll pop up next. Sure, you get a couple of seconds of invincibility, but that’s hardly enough to save this mode.

Map selection will always be contentious when a Call of Duty game launches. Some players will call them inventive and fun while others will say they’re more of the same. I'm in the latter camp, as the only map that does anything exciting is Kill Block, with its shifting, evolving nature. Sadly, that’s only available as a 10 vs. 10 map, so traditional 6 vs. 6 players won’t even see it.

However, even if no map in the normal rotation stands out as exceptionally good, none stand out as outright bad. Each map is good enough to have fun shooting enemies across, and that’s really all I’m looking for (though, like most COD launches, spawn points need a tweak, as I’ve had a few times where I died and spawned right in an enemy’s field of view). Hopefully this will be one of the first things IW fixes with the inevitable post-launch patches.

My favorite mode has always been, and always will be, Team Deathmatch. There’s something pure about two teams of six going head-to-head to see who can eliminate the other side more. But I’ve also enjoyed some Domination, another staple of the COD games. Fortunately, Infinity Ward kept these and all the other staples intact for Modern Warfare 4 (Kill Confirmed, Search and Destroy, Hardpoint, etc.). If you’re coming into this game looking for the stuff you already know you love, I can assure you it’s all there and just as good as ever.

I love Modern Warfare 4. I’m confident I’ll keep playing this version of Call of Duty through the rest of 2026 and deep into 2027, until the next game in the annualized series drops (with a break to follow soon for Grand Theft Auto VI).

Infinity Ward has reminded everyone that it is the “A” developer of Call of Duty, and Modern Warfare 4 will be a tough act for Raven, Treyarch and Sledgehammer to follow. All three modes are fun, and the campaign sucked me in and kept me playing, as none have since the original Modern Warfare 2 (which I still stand by as the best COD campaign ever released). I’d go so far as to say this is in the top three COD campaigns of all time.

Add in the multiplayer and the extraction-based DMZ mode, and you have a well-rounded Call of Duty package that will please fans. It probably won’t convince people who already don’t like COD, but lapsed fans and hardcore players will find plenty to keep them coming back again and again.

#3420. Here’s everything new Apple TV has coming in November

Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery.

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

In the latest special under the acclaimed “Snoopy Presents” banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

#3419. Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

The Democratic Party won total control of Congress in the midterm elections, part of a seismic, nationwide rebuke of Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

The party was widely expected to win back control of the House of Representatives, but less certain was the balance of the Senate. Democrats won them both, though, as part of a hugely successful night capping off one of the most chaotic, contested, and bitter midterm elections in recent history.

Riding a wave of voter turnout amid an economic crisis started by Republican President Donald Trump, Democratic Senate candidates won big in battleground states like Michigan, Georgia, and Maine, as well as in traditionally red states like Texas, Kansa, and South Carolina.

With a majority in the Senate and House, Democrats are now free to pursue an ambitious legislative agenda during Trump’s last two years in office. Trump is entering his lame duck period as a deeply unpopular president beset by scandal and crises of his own making. While he will likely use his presidential veto to keep many of a Democratic Congress’ bills from passing, control over both Houses will give the Democrats a powerful platform to both investigate Trump’s actions in the first half of his second term and set the tone for their agenda going into the next open presidential election in 2028.

“They will turn every committee of Congress into an investigative body, and they’ll go after the president’s family, the Cabinet, his donors and friends,” Speaker of the House Mike Johnson told a room of Christian conservatives earlier this year. “Half of you in this room will be targeted. I run the protection program. I’ll take care of you,” he added.

In the House, the powerful House Oversight Committee is ready to go to work. Their primary target may be Donald Trump’s family businesses, which have dramatically increased in value since the beginning of his second term.

“Every day, Trump gives Congress something new to investigate,” Democratic Rep. Greg Caesar told Rolling Stone last month. “Democrats need to be ready to dig into any and all of it on day one.”

With the Senate under their control, the House’s investigative power gets more support in the upper house of Congress. While Democrats will likely still be far short of the two-thirds supermajority needed to convict Trump in any future impeachment trial, they’ll have enough sway to make sure that any charges the House brings won’t be laughed off by a sycophantic GOP.  Trending Stories Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and 'You Can See Everything' Mick Jagger Praises Sam Fender’s Rolling Stones Cover Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

The balance of the Supreme Court, too, could change as a result of the blue wave. Justice Samuel Alito is nearing retirement, and had the Republicans retained control of the Senate, it was possible Alito would have let Trump fill his fourth vacancy on the court before leaving office in 2029.

All of these battles, however, are still to come. But for tonight, the Democrats must feel as though they’re a little bit closer to winning American politics’ endless war.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3415. Keisha Lance Bottoms Makes History as First Black Woman Elected Governor

Keisha Lance Bottoms has won the Georgia governor’s race, becoming the first Black female governor elected in the United States. Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire businessman Rick Jackson, marking the first time the swing state has elected a Democratic governor in more than two decades.

The victory was a highlight in a massively successful night for Democrats in one of the most bitter midterm elections in recent history, one that saw the Democratic Party win total control of Congress in a nationwide rebuke of Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

Democratic Senate candidates won big in battleground states including Georgia, where Jon Ossoff was re-elected; Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton; and South Carolina, where pediatrician Annie Andrews claimed the South Carolina Senate seat. In another historic first, Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire’s U.S. Senate race, and will be the first openly gay male senator with his victory over Republican John Sununu.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor who also served as an adviser in the Biden administration, won despite a colossal spending disadvantage against Jackson, who pumped tens of millions of his own fortune into his campaign.

Bottoms, like other Democrats across the nation, wielded frustration over the Trump administration to bolster a campaign that remained tightly focused on taking on the rising cost of living and quality of life issues. She also proposed doing away with the state income tax for public school teachers and the state’s tax on car insurance premiums, homeowner’s insurance, and gas. Bottoms also vowed to expand Medicaid and to pause the construction of new data centers in Georgia. #3414. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

Ok, great, but…then no one lists these keyboard shortcuts. Sure would have been helpful to paste them in here when talking about new features.

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

#3413. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3411. New report on ‘HomeView Ultra’ product covers features, pricing, more

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

#3408. Abdul El-Sayed Wins in Michigan, Becomes First Muslim Elected to Senate

Abdul El-Sayed has defeated MAGA Republican Mike Rogers in the race for Michigan’s open Senate seat. The win caps a remarkable run for the insurgent progressive — who ran on bringing prices down, making healthcare available for all, and AI regulation — and marks a significant blow to Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

El-Sayed will become the first Muslim senator in American history.

The race to replace outgoing Sen. Gary Peters — Democrat — became one of the most vitriolic of the cycle. El-Sayed, a Michigan native and epidemiological physician, was subjected to a barrage of attacks against his Muslim faith and Arab heritage.

Trump and Republicans accused El Sayed of having ties to terrorist groups — including claims that he and his mother were associated with the Muslim Brotherhood. Republicans — and some Democrats — also attempted to frame El-Sayed’s campaign activities alongside leftist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as a signal of his supposed extremist ideology. At campaign events, Trump continuously mocked El-Sayed’s heritage and name at rallies. Just a week before Election Day, Trump referred to El-Sayed as a “Jihadist Member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” who wanted to institute “Sharia Law” in the United States. Rogers seized on similar lines of attack after winning his own primary, even as he attempted to distance himself from Trump by calling for an end to his trade war with Canada.

Democrats countered with the big guns. Former President Barack Obama campaigned alongside El-Sayed in his tour of contested states, which included Michigan, Ohio, and Georgia. Obama mocked Trump’s obsession with asses and jaw lines and the male physique, and his fixation on remodeling and redecorating the White House.

“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said of the Senate candidate, drawing comparisons to the right’s attempts to question his own heritage and faith during his presidency.

One Democrat who didn’t get behind El-Sayed was his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. Throughout the primary, Stevens accused El-Sayed of wanting to “blame all of [his] problems on Jewish Americans” in response to their policy difference over the war in Gaza. The divisions of the primary lingered through the general, and though she for months insisted she supported the Democratic ticket, she formally endorsed Rogers in a shocking move two days before the election. #3407. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.
